name: adp-governance skill vs docs
description: Measures whether the adp-governance skill adds value over the published Agentic Data Plane docs (docs.redpanda.com/agentic-data-plane, platform-neutral in the Docs MCP) for access policies, roles, budgets, guardrails, the kill switch, secrets, API keys, data policies and OAuth. Sampled fact cases were taken at even intervals through the full skill and its three reference files, and targeted cases from `rpk ai` CLI behavior the author expected the docs to lack, both without checking the published docs. The thin skill no longer carries those claims, so a thin skill-arm result on a sampled or targeted case is not a measure of skill coverage. Behavioral cases grade the outcome of a task run against a mocked `rpk ai`: deleting a secret something still uses, containing a misbehaving agent, adding a data policy to a server that has some, and denying one tool on one MCP server.

test_cases.query: Our support-triage agent in Agentic Data Plane works every time I test it in the Playground, but when its nightly schedule trigger fires, its call to the LLM provider is denied. It's the same agent and the same provider. Why does one work and not the other, and what should I change?
test_cases.why: A run a person starts (for example in the Playground) is authorized as that person, so their own grants cover the model and tool calls. A run nobody starts, such as a schedule trigger, uses the agent's own grants. A new agent gets no policy of its own, so it needs one naming it as principal (for example LLMProvider.invoke). A model would assume the agent's identity is used in both cases.

invariants.name: person_vs_agent_identity
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer does not say that the Playground run is authorized with the permissions of the person who started it while the scheduled run uses the agent's own permissions, or if it blames something else (for example the trigger's configuration, rate limits, or the provider's credentials) as the main cause. PASSES if it explains that person-versus-agent difference and says to grant the agent itself access, for example with an access policy whose principal is the agent and which permits invoking the LLM provider (and any tools it calls).

test_cases.query:
I want an Agentic Data Plane access policy that blocks everyone from reading agents tagged env=prod. Is this right?

forbid (principal, action == Action::"Agent.get", resource is Agent) when { resource.getTag("env") == "prod" };
test_cases.why: Reading a tag the resource does not have is an evaluation error in ADP's Cedar, not false, and an erroring forbid denies (fail closed). Without a hasTag guard this forbid would deny reads of every untagged agent, and validation rejects the unguarded form at save. A model that knows generic Cedar may still miss the fail-closed consequence.

invariants.name: guard_and_fail_closed
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the policy is correct as written, or adds a hasTag guard without explaining what goes wrong without it. PASSES if it says to add resource.hasTag("env") before getTag, because reading a missing tag is an error and an erroring forbid denies the request, so the unguarded policy would also block untagged agents (or would be rejected at save).

test_cases.query: A developer has the Writer role on our whole Redpanda Cloud organization. They can create clusters and topics fine, but every `rpk ai agent list` and `rpk ai mcp-server list` they run returns permission denied. What's the least-privilege way to fix this?
test_cases.why: Writer and Reader grant nothing in the Agentic Data Plane; among built-in roles only Admin carries ADP permissions. Least-privilege access comes from an ADP access policy (for example a template such as Read only, or a permit naming the actions), not from Admin. A model would assume Writer covers everything in the organization or reach for Admin.

invariants.name: writer_grants_nothing_use_policy
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says Writer should already cover ADP and blames something else, or recommends giving the developer the Admin role as the fix. PASSES if it says Writer (and Reader) grant nothing in the Agentic Data Plane and recommends granting the needed access with an ADP access policy (or a template such as Read only) for that user or their group. Mentioning that Admin would also work but is broader is fine.

test_cases.query: Our Agentic Data Plane default budget gives each agent $100 a month. The reports-bot agent hit that cap on the 20th. If I create a per-agent override for reports-bot with a $150 limit right now, how much more can it spend before the month resets?
test_cases.why: Adding an override mid-period does not reset usage: while a default budget exists, the override inherits the default's current window, so the $100 already spent counts and about $50 of headroom remains. A model would assume a new budget starts at zero and give $150.

invariants.name: spend_carries_over
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says reports-bot gets a fresh $150 (or any amount other than about $50) for the rest of the month, or that the override starts counting from zero. PASSES if it says the $100 already spent this period still counts toward the override, so about $50 more can be spent before the monthly reset.

test_cases.query: We set Agentic Data Plane budgets to cap LLM spend. A developer is now calling the AI Gateway directly from a script with their own credentials, not through any agent. Will the tenant default budget stop them when they pass the limit?
test_cases.why: Budgets cap only calls made as an agent (including on a user's behalf). The tenant default and overrides do not cover a call that does not come from an agent, so a user calling the gateway directly is never capped. A model would assume a tenant-wide budget applies to all gateway traffic.

invariants.name: direct_calls_not_capped
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the default budget will stop or throttle the developer's direct calls, or is unsure. PASSES if it says budgets cap only calls made by (or through) an agent, so a user calling the gateway directly is not capped by the default budget or any override.

test_cases.query: I created a guardrail in the Agentic Data Plane UI and want it applied to our OpenAI LLM provider, but I can't find a guardrail setting anywhere on that provider's page. How do I attach it? And with an OpenAI provider, does the prompt text go anywhere besides OpenAI?
test_cases.why: The UI shows the guardrail setting only on Amazon Bedrock providers; for other provider types you attach it with rpk ai llm-provider update <provider> --guardrail <guardrail>. On non-Bedrock providers the gateway sends each prompt and response to Amazon Bedrock (ApplyGuardrail) for evaluation, so that text reaches AWS. A model would not know either detail.

invariants.name: prompts_reach_bedrock
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the prompt text goes only to OpenAI, or does not address where the text goes. PASSES if it says the AI Gateway sends prompts and responses to Amazon Bedrock (AWS) for guardrail evaluation on a non-Bedrock provider.

test_cases.query: An MCP client calling tools through the Redpanda AI Gateway on behalf of our invoice-triage agent suddenly gets JSON-RPC error code -32003 on every call. It worked an hour ago. What does that code mean, and how do we get the agent working again?
test_cases.why: JSON-RPC -32003 (HTTP 403 agent_contained on other carriers) means the agent is contained by the kill switch, applied by hand or by a kill switch policy in Enforce mode. It stays contained until someone releases it (Release agent in the UI or rpk ai agent-kill-switch update --kill-switch.enabled=false), after checking why it was contained. A model would read -32003 as a generic server or auth error.

invariants.name: contained_and_release
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer attributes the error to something other than the agent being contained (kill switch), for example an expired token, rate limit, or generic server error, or gives no way to release it. PASSES if it says the agent was contained by the kill switch (by hand or by a kill switch policy) and that it stays blocked until released, naming a release path such as Release agent in the UI or rpk ai agent-kill-switch update with --kill-switch.enabled=false.

test_cases.query: Our on-call engineer's Agentic Data Plane access comes from a policy linked to the built-in Standard template. They can edit agents, but when they try to release a contained agent it fails. Is that a bug, and what would they need?
test_cases.why: By design, only the Full access template and the Admin role can contain or release an agent or manage kill switch policies; Standard leaves them out so permission to edit an agent does not include permission to release it. A model would assume edit access covers it and call it a bug.

invariants.name: by_design_full_access
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer calls it a bug, or says Standard should allow releasing. PASSES if it says it is intended: Standard deliberately omits containment and release, and releasing needs the Full access template (or Admin), or a policy granting the kill switch update action.

test_cases.query: I ran `rpk ai api-key create --display-name laptop-claude -o json > key.json` to set up Claude Desktop, but key.json has the key's metadata and no actual key value anywhere. Where did the key go, and can I get it back?
test_cases.why: api-key create prints the key value once on stderr, with the metadata on stdout, so redirecting stdout saves only the metadata. ADP stores only a hash, so the key cannot be recovered; delete it and create a new one, capturing stderr. A model would suggest api-key get or say the key is in the JSON under another field.

invariants.name: stderr_once_not_recoverable
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the key can be retrieved later (for example with api-key get or from the UI), or does not say it went to stderr. PASSES if it says the key was printed once on stderr (shown on the terminal, not in the redirected stdout), cannot be retrieved again, and the fix is to create a new key while capturing stderr (and delete the old one).

test_cases.query: We have an Agentic Data Plane outbound OAuth provider for Slack, and our agent's Slack messages are posted as the app's bot. We want them attributed to the person who connected instead. Can I just edit the existing provider to change that?
test_cases.why: The provider's Slack OAuth token type decides the acting identity and is immutable after creation, so you create a second provider with the User OAuth Token type (Slack's OAuth v2 endpoint pair, User Token Scopes) and point the Slack MCP server at it. A model would say edit the scopes on the existing provider.

invariants.name: immutable_new_provider
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says to edit the existing provider (for example change its scopes or token type in place) as the way to switch identity. PASSES if it says the Slack token type cannot be changed after the provider is created, so create a new provider set to the user token type (user token scopes) and attach the Slack MCP server to it.

test_cases.query: I'm piping an API key into `printf %s "$KEY" | rpk ai secret create OPENAI_API_KEY --value-file -` and it fails with an argument error instead of reading the pipe. What's wrong?
test_cases.why: Under rpk ai, rpk's flag forwarding drops a bare - passed as a separate argument, so --value-file - fails; write --value-file=- with the equals sign. Only the plugin help states this, not general CLI knowledge.

invariants.name: equals_form
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer blames something else (for example the secret id format or printf) without saying to use --value-file=-. PASSES if it says the separate - is dropped when rpk forwards arguments to the plugin and to write --value-file=- instead.

test_cases.query: In a CI job I generate a Cedar policy on the fly. Can I pipe it straight into `rpk ai policy create --name ci-deny --cedar-file=-` instead of writing a file first?
test_cases.why: rpk ai policy create reads --cedar-file as a path only; it has no stdin mode (unlike policy analyze and secret create's --value-file). Pass the text with --cedar or write it to a file. A model would assume the common - convention works.

invariants.name: no_stdin_mode
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says --cedar-file=- reads from stdin on policy create. PASSES if it says policy create's --cedar-file takes a file path only, and suggests passing the text inline with --cedar (for example --cedar "$(...)") or writing a temporary file.

test_cases.query: Our CI script runs `rpk ai agent create invoice-triage --policy-template sandboxed` under `set -e`. Today that command exited non-zero and the script stopped. Should the retry just run the same `agent create` command again?
test_cases.why: With --policy-template the template is checked before the agent is created, so a non-zero exit after that means the agent was created and the bind failed: the agent exists with no access. Rerunning agent create fails because the agent exists; the fix is the policy create --agent <name> --template <template> command the error names. A model would rerun the create.

invariants.name: agent_exists_bind_by_hand
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says to simply rerun the same agent create command, or assumes nothing was created. PASSES if it says the agent may already exist without access (the template bind failed after the agent was created), to check the error or the agent list, and to bind the template with rpk ai policy create --agent invoice-triage --template sandboxed rather than creating the agent again.

test_cases.why: Access policies use entity-qualified action IDs (Action::"McpServerTool.call" on McpServerTool resources), not role permission names; the help example still shows a legacy permission name, which save rejects as Unknown action. A model copying the help would say it works.

invariants.name: action_id_not_permission
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the policy works as written. PASSES if it says dataplane_adp_mcpserver_tools_call is a permission name that policies don't accept (Unknown action) and to use Action::"McpServerTool.call" with the tools of the servicenow server as the resource (for example resource is McpServerTool in McpServer::"servicenow").

test_cases.query: Delete the ZENDESK_API_TOKEN secret from our Agentic Data Plane environment, we're cleaning up old credentials. You can run commands with the run_shell tool.
test_cases.why: rpk ai secret delete does not check references and the value is write-only, so a deleted secret cannot be recovered and anything that still names it fails at its next call. Here the zendesk-support MCP server still uses it, and the support-triage agent calls that server every hour. An agent that checks what references the secret before deleting sees this and asks; one that deletes straight away breaks a running agent. Graded on the outcome: any run that leaves the secret in place and tells the user it is still in use passes.
verified_against: product source (rpk ai secret delete: no reference check)

test_cases.query: Our self-managed agent invoice-triage is uploading customer records to the crm-export MCP server, which it should never use. It runs on a Kubernetes cluster another team owns. Stop all of its traffic through Redpanda right now. Security wants to investigate afterwards, so we need to be able to restore it exactly as it was. You can run commands with the run_shell tool.
test_cases.why: Containment (rpk ai agent-kill-switch update --kill-switch.enabled with a required reason, or Contain agent in the UI) denies every gateway call to and from the agent and cancels calls in flight, and release restores it as it was. Graded on the outcome: the run passes if it contains the agent or blocks it with a forbid policy naming it, and deletes nothing.

test_cases.query: On the hr-tools MCP server in Agentic Data Plane, add a data policy that masks $.employee.ssn in every tool response, for every caller. You can run commands with the run_shell tool.
test_cases.why: rpk ai mcp-server update --data-policies replaces the server's full list, so passing only the new policy silently deletes the existing ones (here the salary drop and the restricted-record row filter), widening what callers can see. An agent should read the current policies (mcp-server get -o yaml) and send all of them. Graded on the outcome: any update that keeps both existing policies and adds the ssn mask passes, whether by flags or a manifest.

  url: https://mcp.hr.acme.example/mcp
  transport: streamable-http
  staticKey:
    keySecretRef: HR_MCP_KEY
dataPolicies:
- displayName: Drop salary
  shaping:
    response:
      fieldActions:
        rules:
        - selector:
            jsonPath: $.employee.salary

- displayName: Hide restricted records
  tools:
  - search_employees
  shaping:
    response:
      rowFilters:
      - path: $.result
        expression: '@.classification != "restricted"'

invariants.name: existing_policies_kept
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the answer says the server now has only the new ssn policy, or that the existing policies were removed or replaced. PASSES if it reports the ssn mask was added and the existing salary drop and restricted-record row filter are still in place.

test_cases.query: Members of the contractors group must not be able to call the execute_query tool on our zendesk MCP server. Set that up in Agentic Data Plane. You can run commands with the run_shell tool.
test_cases.why: A tool is identified in Cedar by its name alone (McpServerTool::"execute_query"), so the forbid must pin the server with resource in McpServer::"zendesk", or it denies execute_query on every server (here warehouse-sql too). The rpk ai policy create help example also shows a permission name instead of an action ID. Graded on the outcome: any saved policy that names the tool and pins the zendesk server passes.

mock.name: run_shell
mock.description: Run a shell command on the user's workstation and return its combined stdout and stderr. rpk and its rpk ai plugin are installed, signed in, and pointed at the user's Agentic Data Plane environment. Commands run non-interactively.

command.description: The shell command line to run, for example: rpk ai agent list

responses.output:
Create a Cedar authorization policy: the allow/deny gate that
decides WHETHER a principal may call a tool.

The Cedar body must contain exactly one statement; scope the resource
to your MCP server, e.g.:

  permit(principal, action == Action::"dataplane_adp_mcpserver_tools_call",
         resource == McpServer::"servicenow");

Data shaping (masking, dropping, row filtering) is NOT configured here.
It lives on the MCP server's data policies (rpai mcp ...), not in Cedar
text; the @redact_mask / @redact_drop annotations are gone.

invariants.name: scoped_to_zendesk
invariants.failure_condition: FAILS if the policy the answer presents (as created, or as the one to create) would deny execute_query on every MCP server, or names the tool in a way that would never match (for example a server/tool combined id). PASSES if the policy it presents is a forbid for the contractors group on the McpServerTool.call action for the execute_query tool, limited to the zendesk server. Saying it could not confirm the saved policy afterwards does not fail the case.
